result.what_it_is: A short beginner tutorial (Part 1 only, by Ayoub Ennaoui, published 2025-04-19) on streaming JSON over a FastAPI WebSocket to a future Angular page. The whole backend is one endpoint, /ws/odds, that sends RANDOM numbers for a placeholder "Team A vs Team B" every 3 seconds. It uses no odds API, no vendor, no scraper, no database and no real bookmaker data. Part 2 (the Angular client) is announced but I found no sign it was ever published. I read the full body text on 2026-10-07 from the author's public Medium RSS feed (https://medium.com/feed/@ayoubennaoui20, HTTP 200). The article page itself returned a Cloudflare challenge (403) and I did not work around it.
result.upstream_data_source: None. The "odds" are generated in the server loop with random.uniform(1.5, 2.5). The author says so: "To keep things simple and focused on WebSocket functionality, we simulate the odds data instead of calling an external API or accessing a database." The code has no HTTP client, no vendor key and no odds provider. load_dotenv() and os are imported but nothing reads an API key. No other upstream is named anywhere in the text.
result.push_or_poll: Server-to-browser PUSH over a WebSocket, but timer-driven rather than change-driven: a per-connection "while True" loop does send_json() then asyncio.sleep(3), whether or not anything changed. There is no upstream poll or push because there is no upstream. If a real feed were bolted on, a viewer would see that feed's age plus up to 3 s (INFERRED from the loop).
result.claimed_latency_or_refresh: Only prose and a code comment. Prose: "Every second matters — the odds are shifting based on goals, red cards, substitutions". Comment: "# simulate new odds every 3 seconds". The article states no latency number for any real feed because it uses none. It also says WebSockets "Reduce latency and bandwidth usage", a generic claim that says nothing about how fresh a price is.
result.measured_or_verified_age: None. The payload is {"match": ..., "odds": {"Team A": float, "Team B": float}} with no timestamp, no bookmaker and no market id. There is no real price, so it has no age. No third-party measurement exists, because the code is a demo.
result.coverage: None. One hard-coded fake matchup with two random decimal numbers. No sports, leagues, players, props, books or sharp-book prices. No live in-play odds and no scores.
result.price_and_free_tier: Free to read. The code needs only Python 3.9+, fastapi and uvicorn, which are free and open source. There is no data plan or free tier because there is no data vendor. The article mentions Firestore (optional) and Chart.js (optional), neither of which is an odds source. Read 2026-10-07.
result.terms_notes: I did not read Medium's terms of service. Medium's article and profile pages answered this container with a Cloudflare challenge (403, title "Attention Required! | Cloudflare"). I did not try to get past it, and I did not use paywall-bypass mirrors. Only the public RSS feed was read, one GET. The tutorial contains no scraping, so scraping clauses do not apply. verdict.why: This is not an odds or scores source. It is a toy WebSocket demo that streams random numbers every 3 seconds, with no vendor, no upstream and no timestamp. It is free only because it has no data, so it cannot beat CNO or the Novig makers. The technique is a FastAPI WebSocket relay that fans a feed out to browsers (Angular). Vigilant is a single-user Android app that can open the upstream sockets or REST polls itself (Polymarket, Sofascore and so on), so a relay would only add a hop, a host and latency. The tutorial's timer loop also decouples send time from change time, the opposite of what the bar needs. Even if a real feed were swapped in, a viewer would see that feed's age plus up to 3 s. Nothing here needs further research and nothing here needs a phone test. The real question is which upstream to relay, and this article does not answer it.

result.what_it_is: "BkSignal API": a small, anonymous, pay-per-product JSON HTTP polling API (Laravel/Apache site, registered 2022-07-30 at Namecheap, bksignal.com serves the same page) that relays live (in-play) and prematch main-market odds, plus an optional live score block, from 22 Russian/CIS, European and crypto/offshore bookmakers (Fonbet, Olimp, Leonbets, Ligastavok, Winline, Baltbet, Bwin, Zenit, Betboom, Maxline, 1Win, Nordicbet, 1xbet, Vbet, WinlineKz, Vave, Cloudbet, Stake, Bcgame, Cryptorino, Roobet, Bcgame Ru lang). It is not an odds-comparison page and not a tipster "signal" service despite the name. Sports: Football (not defined; Cyrillic team names in the docs suggest soccer), Basketball, Tennis, Volleyball, IceHockey, TableTennis. Only Fonbet, Ligastavok and Winline carry all six sports; Bwin, Stake and Bcgame carry basketball and volleyball; the other 16 carry live basketball only. Read 2026-10-07 (page text, JSON-LD and docs all read in raw HTML; the page has no date stamp). No GitHub repo, changelog, status page, about page, or terms found; searching the domain name returned nothing from any third party.
result.upstream_data_source: Not stated anywhere. The home page only says "Structured sports odds data via API. Coverage is shown by sport and market type" and lists bookmaker names as data sources. Docs describe `updated_at` as "when the event was updated according to our data (UTC)", which is BkSignal's own stamp, not the bookmaker's. INFERRED: it scrapes or sockets into each bookmaker's own public site/app (the bookmaker is the key in the response, 'Currently supported from the main table', and the docs say 'opponents ... in the same order as on the bookmaker website'; the example shows a Cyrillic team name list). So it is a scraper-reseller of consumer bookmaker feeds, which is the thing this project's rules say never to do itself. It does not name a licensed feed (Sportradar, Genius, etc.).
result.push_or_poll: Poll only. HTTPS GET with the API key inside the URL path. Docs mention no websocket, SSE or push. Incremental polling is supported through an updateVersion Unix-seconds path segment (server returns only records with updated_at > updateVersion; next call uses result.updateVersion from the last response).
result.claimed_latency_or_refresh: Marketing only: the home page labels feeds "Live Realtime odds" and "Upcoming Prematch odds"; no millisecond or second figure for data age. The docs only give the polling budget: "Rate limit: no more than 1 request per second" and "Recommended polling: every 2-5 seconds for Live odds and every 30 seconds for Upcoming odds". The docs state no refresh rate for the underlying data.
result.measured_or_verified_age: none. I did not request any odds payload: every data call needs an API key obtained by registering (email/password plus Telegram username form), and the rules forbid sign-ups, and the key-in-path endpoints are not documented as keyless. What is verified is only the schema: each event carries an `updated_at` (ISO 8601, UTC, whole seconds, e.g. "2026-01-23T11:34:55Z") that is BkSignal's own update time, not the bookmaker's time or the play time, so even with a key it would only prove how old BkSignal's copy is. I could not check the payload time against the HTTP Date header.
result.coverage: Raw HTML of the home page (92 KB), the /docs page (35 KB), /register (GET, not submitted), /robots.txt, the JSON-LD blocks and the RDAP record for bksignal.com. Everything on the site was read; the site is tiny (home, docs, register, login). 9 requests to odds.bksignal.com in total, at least 1 second apart, plus 1 to rdap.org. result.price_and_free_tier: Read 2026-10-07 from the home page: "$5 / 30 days" listed against every bookmaker x sport x category line (Live "Realtime odds" and Upcoming "Prematch odds" are listed as separate $5 items, INFERRED to be separate products; the page does not say whether a key covers many items). FAQ: "Can I try the sports odds API for free? Yes. A free trial is available, but the number of events is limited to two." The documented test endpoint returns up to 2 current events for all supported bookmakers and is limited to 1 request per 30 seconds. No pricing page, no request quotas per month, no stated payment methods (a `heleket` meta tag, a crypto payment gateway's site-verification tag, hints that payment is cryptocurrency; INFERRED). Live and Upcoming are in the paid and trial products; sockets do not exist.
result.terms_notes: No terms of service, privacy policy, acceptable-use or redistribution text found: /terms and /privacy return 404, the register form has only password, confirm password and Telegram username fields and no terms link, and the docs/home pages have no such section. robots.txt is "User-agent: *  Disallow:" (allows all). Docs contain one operational restriction: error code ip_locked, 'Requests are allowed only from the bound IP. If you try from a new IP, wait for the cooldown 1 minute and retry.' That is a serious fit problem for a phone app on a mobile network with changing IPs: it would need a fixed-IP relay server. The vendor is anonymous (no company, address, contact other than Telegram at sign-up), so there is no legal basis for betting use, no SLA, and no way to learn what data rights it has.

verdict.why: It is cheap ($5 per 30 days per line) but it does not give Vigilant a fair-price source. ODDS: none of its 22 books is a sharp or US book (no Pinnacle, Circa, Kalshi, ProphetX, Sporttrade, Novig), it has no baseball or NFL/college, no props, only main markets, and its prices come from Russian/CIS/crypto retail books, so they cannot say what Novig's price should be. A 2-5 s poll with an `updated_at` stamp is the right shape, but that stamp is only BkSignal's own copy time, so it cannot prove the underlying price's age; no measurement was possible without a key (registration forbidden), so freshness versus CNO is unknown, not assumed. SCORES: its `scores` block is the only thing worth a thought: live scores come from some books (documented examples only basketball and volleyball) and are 'not always' present; Fonbet/Ligastavok/Winline carry tennis, and a Russian book's live score could in principle lead Novig's re-quote, but nothing proves it, and the project already has Sofascore REST at 2.5 s with a measured median 6.4 s lead on the tennis score socket and 22 of 29 Novig-moving scores >= 3 s early, which this cannot be shown to beat. It is a third-party scraper reseller of bookmakers' consumer feeds (the technique this project forbids doing itself), anonymous operator, no terms, no SLA, key bound to one IP (a phone on mobile data would need a fixed-IP relay), and nobody writes about it anywhere I could find. Net: not a rapid odds source for Vigilant; at best a speculative, unverified score probe for tennis, worth only a $5 test if Tj wants one and only through a fixed-IP relay.

what_the_phone_should_test: Nothing is worth testing on the odds side: the source has no sharp or US book, so a speed test would not change the verdict.

Optional $5 score probe only if Tj wants to close the question: buy one 30-day Live Tennis line for Fonbet (carries tennis, with scores only if Fonbet's main table has them), and poll it from a fixed-IP relay at 1 request per second (the key is IP-bound, so the phone's mobile IP will return `ip_locked`). Log (a) whether `scores` exists for live tennis at all, (b) the `updated_at` per event against the phone's clock, and (c) the time the score changes versus Sofascore REST at 2.5 s and versus Novig's moneyline re-quote on the same match. Judge by the same bar as RESEARCH.md section 99: the score must show at least 3 s before Novig's price moves on the large majority of Novig-moving points. If scores are absent on tennis (likely, since docs examples show only basketball and volleyball), stop.

result.what_it_is: A vendor advertisement written as a tutorial. It was published 2026-05-21T13:06:54Z (dateModified is identical) and I read it 2026-10-07. The byline is "E. Mitev". It argues for using an aggregator API instead of scraping Bet365, FanDuel and DraftKings, and it recommends and uses one vendor, PulseScore (pulsescore.net, api.pulsescore.net). The code is two short Python snippets. One polls pre-match odds over REST with an X-Secret header. The other prints frames from a WebSocket. The article is an ad. The author's DEV profile reads "We provide real-time sports odds from Bet365, Paddy Power & more via API ... Free tier available - no credit card needed", with website pulsescore.net and Twitter handle @pulsescoreapi. The account was created 2026-05-21, the same day as the post, and has 8 posts that all promote PulseScore. This post has no disclosure line, 0 reactions and 0 comments. A later post by the same account (2026-10-06) does say "Disclosure: We build PulseScore." The same vendor is probably behind other sources in this batch (items 8 and 10 point to pulsescore.net).
result.upstream_data_source: PulseScore's own scrapers of bookmakers' consumer sites. They write into a database (the stream doc says "seq is the Mongo cluster time"), and PulseScore serves that copy over REST, a per-bookmaker WebSocket and a delta-stream WebSocket. It is not a licensed feed and not a book's own socket. Evidence (all VERIFIED on the vendor's own pages): the homepage says "Live betting odds from soccer and tennis - scraped from top bookmakers and updated every second"; the PS3838 Swagger text says "The scraper rewrites every event it still tracks on each pass"; the vendor's blog post says "we thought we were building a collection of scrapers ... Most of the engineering effort went into reliability, normalization, monitoring". The Terms call the data "aggregated publicly available sports betting odds data" from "third-party bookmaker sources". The Kalshi and Polymarket entries are derived rather than copied. The Kalshi Swagger text says "decimal odds derived from the last traded price plus the current best bid/ask" (CLAIM_ONLY). The article's thesis is "stop scraping", but the product it sells is a scrape run by someone else. The vendor's own post lists endpoints disappearing and Cloudflare updates as a recurring problem, so the upstream can break without notice (INFERRED).
result.push_or_poll: There are three ways in. (1) REST polling: free BASIC is 500 requests a month at 1 request/s per bookmaker; the article's first snippet is this one. (2) A legacy per-bookmaker, per-sport WebSocket (wss://api.pulsescore.net/api/{bookmaker}/ws/live?key=..&sport=..) that pushes a frame about every second with every live event for that sport; PRO and above only. (3) A Stream API (Beta, protocol v2, wss://api.pulsescore.net/api/stream/ws) that sends one snapshot and then keyed deltas, batched once a second, with a seq number and a 120 s resume window; also PRO and above. The article's second snippet (the socket) cannot work on the free key the article tells readers to use. Pricing page, Terms and docs all put sockets on PRO and above. The docs say BASIC and STARTER handshakes are rejected with close code 4003.
result.claimed_latency_or_refresh: Marketing claims only. The article says "Live events update every 1 second" and "a 1-2 second refresh rate". The homepage says "refreshed every ~1 second". The stream page says "Every odds change, the moment it lands." The vendor's own stream doc is more modest: "Changes are batched once per second per stream, so a delta typically arrives 1-2 seconds after the bookmaker's write; this is not a sub-second feed." The October tutorial adds that the one-second cadence "is not a guarantee that every bookmaker price reaches your application within one second." It also says "We have not tested this wrapper against the authenticated live service. This tutorial does not report a live latency benchmark." A search snippet of the Product Hunt page (second-hand; Product Hunt returned 403 to the container) lists under-1-second live updates as a goal, not a result.
result.measured_or_verified_age:
None. I could not measure the age of any price or score. Reasons:
1. Every odds endpoint needs a key and returns 401 without one ({"message":"User is not authorized"}). I did not sign up, as the rules require.
2. The only keyless endpoint is /api/stream/capabilities, which lists bookmakers and sports. I probed it once. Its discoveredAt (23:31:40Z) was 7 min 38 s older than the response Date header (23:39:19Z), consistent with the docs' "refreshed every 10 minutes". That says nothing about odds age.
3. Even with a key, the vendor documents that its age stamp does not prove price age. The PS3838 Swagger text says every event carries updatedAt, "the time the feed last wrote that document. The scraper rewrites every event it still tracks on each pass, so read it as a freshness stamp for the document rather than as the moment a price last moved."
4. The stream protocol never sends updatedAt, markets[].updatedAt or oddsSig ("Never sent, never diffed"), and the vendor's Python client drops them (_IGNORED_TOP and _IGNORED_MARKET). The delta frame's "ts" can only show PulseScore-to-client delay.
5. The pass interval of the scraper is not stated anywhere I read.
6. I found no third-party latency measurement, Reddit or HN thread, GitHub issue or Trustpilot page. The sportsapis.dev review says its ratings come from "directory research" (not hands-on tests), and its connection and rate figures for ULTRA are out of date.
result.coverage:
PulseScore lists 58 bookmakers (the /api/stream/capabilities list I fetched 2026-10-07), including the US books FanDuel, DraftKings, BetMGM (US), BetRivers, Hard Rock Bet, BetPARX, Borgata, Bovada and BetOnline.

Player props: not documented for the US books. The sportsapis.dev review says "There is no mention of player props", and I found no props wording in the FanDuel, Kalshi or PS3838 Swagger texts. A few non-US books' blurbs mention props (Winamax ES, Interwetten).

Live scores: live events carry score, matchClock and periodScores "when the bookmaker provides it ... Some books publish odds only". For PS3838 the stored score is "the last score and match clock PS3838 published." So scores are the bookmaker's own scoreboard, scraped (VERIFIED wording; the consequence is INFERRED). Kalshi has no score field.
result.price_and_free_tier:
Read on the pricing page and Terms §3-4 on 2026-10-07. Terms are marked "Last updated: October 7, 2026".

| Plan | Price | Requests | Rate (per bookmaker) | Sockets |
| :- | :- | :- | :- | :- |
| BASIC | free | 500 requests a month | 1 request/s | none |
| STARTER | €20 a month | 30,000 requests a month | 1 request/min | none |
| PRO | €79 a month (€395 per 6 months, €711 per 12 months) | unlimited | 1 request/s | 1 WebSocket per bookmaker; Stream API 1 connection, 1 sport, all bookmakers |

| ULTRA | €249 a month | unlimited | 6 requests/s | 6 per bookmaker; Stream API 3 connections, all sports |

Further limits and offers:
- There is an absolute cap of 15 requests/s per key.
- The free tier has no live socket and no Stream API. 500 requests is about 16 a day, enough to inspect payload shape and not to run a scan.
- The only plan with a live push is PRO, from €79 a month. That is above the "cheap" line and is not free.
- PRO monthly has a "7 Days Free Trial". Whether a card is needed is not stated.
- Terms §2: paid plans are non-refundable once any API call has been made.
- The Stream API is in Beta, and the vendor says plan limits may still move.
result.terms_notes:
Terms of Service (pulsescore.net/terms, read 2026-10-07), quoted:

- §5: "You agree not to: Resell, redistribute, or sublicense the data obtained through the API without prior written consent. Scrape, crawl, or systematically extract data from the API beyond your plan's intended usage. ... Attempt to circumvent rate limits, authentication, or any security measures."
- §6: "PulseScore aggregates odds data from third-party bookmaker sources. While we strive to provide accurate and timely data, we make no guarantees regarding real-time accuracy, completeness, or availability. ... You use the data entirely at your own risk."
- Nothing forbids using the data for your own betting. The only gambling clause is "facilitate illegal gambling operations".
- Personal use inside Vigilant looks permitted. Passing the data on to other users would not be.
- §7: access can be cut at any time. §9 excludes liability for lost profits.
- Legal and continuity risk is on the upstream side: the sources are consumer sportsbooks that PulseScore scrapes. Their own terms are a separate matter I did not research (INFERRED). PulseScore's own post says endpoints vanish and Cloudflare changes break scrapers.
- Rate limits: ten 429s within ten seconds pauses the key for 60 s.
- Scraping what the article's own targets would break (Bet365, FanDuel, DraftKings): the article names Cloudflare anti-bot, changing HTML, and proxy management. It does not discuss their terms.

verdict.why:
This is an advertisement for PulseScore, not a method.

The free tier cannot be rapid. It is REST only, 500 requests a month, with no socket and no stream. The article's own WebSocket example fails on the free key it tells readers to use.

The cheapest live push is PRO at €79 a month, which is above the cheap line. STARTER at €20 is REST at 1 request/min per bookmaker, so it is worse than CNO.

The data is scraped, and the vendor says so. The age of any price is unprovable. The only freshness stamp, updatedAt, is rewritten on every scrape pass and the vendor says it is not the moment a price moved. The stream strips it out entirely. The vendor's best figure is a delta arriving 1-2 s after its own database write, "not a sub-second feed". The scrape-pass interval is never stated. That is the "real-time claim without a stated age" the bar calls worthless.

Coverage of what Vigilant needs is thin. Only PS3838 (likely Pinnacle's Asian brand), Kalshi and Polymarket overlap with the sharp list. Vigilant already reads Pinnacle (PinnWire/pinnapi), Kalshi and Polymarket directly, so PulseScore would be an extra hop over a scrape of them. It has no Circa, ProphetX, Sporttrade or Novig, and no documented player props. Hockey is not live at PS3838.

Scores are the book's own scoreboard and arrive no earlier than that book's price. They cannot beat Sofascore at 2.5 s, or Polymarket's socket, ahead of Novig's 16 s re-quote. That last point is INFERRED.

The delta-stream design (snapshot, keyed patches, seq, resume) is a sound pattern, but Vigilant's existing push sources already do the same job.

In short, it is unmeasured and probably not ahead of the sources Vigilant already has. Treat it as a €79-a-month, unmeasured, scraped second copy of Pinnacle. Only a 7-day PRO trial plus a free-key comparison could change that, and the free-key test below should settle it first.

what_the_phone_should_test: Free-key spot check, about 10 of the 500 monthly requests. Tj creates a BASIC key himself, since I did not sign up. During a live tennis or basketball game, GET https://api.pulsescore.net/api/ps3838/live-events?sport=tennis (or basketball) with headers X-Secret: <key> and Accept-Encoding: gzip, about 5 s apart, 5 times. Log the HTTP Date header and each event's updatedAt. Expect updatedAt to sit within a few seconds of Date every time (it is rewritten each scrape pass). That shows the scrape cadence and proves nothing about price age.

Price-age test, about 20 requests: in the same minutes, log when the same game's price changes in the PulseScore response versus Vigilant's own Pinnacle read (PinnWire/pinnapi) and its Kalshi read, with phone timestamps. Compute the median lead or lag. A median lead of 3 s or more would be needed for it to matter; a lag means stop.

Score check, a few requests: compare score and matchClock from the same live-events response with Sofascore's REST poll at 2.5 s for the same tennis match. Expect PulseScore later, since it is the book's scoreboard.
Do not try the WebSocket on the free key; the docs say it is rejected with 4003.

Only if the first three tests show a ps3838 lead of 3 s or more over Vigilant's current Pinnacle path: start the PRO 7-day free trial (monthly billing only, card requirement not stated, no refund once any call is made) and open wss://api.pulsescore.net/api/ps3838/ws/live?key=<key>&sport=tennis from the phone for one match. Log frame arrival times against the Pinnacle direct read. Cancel before day 7. Even a good result is €79 a month, above the cheap line.
